checks: A ray from the interior meets the support boundary at most once, so discarding boundary values preserves each weighted ray integral as well as the Lebesgue measure. The finite convex inverse power is continuous on the open positive interior. If it vanishes there, convexity on a surrounding ball gives a radial upper bound linear in distance to the zero, so the original density dominates a nonintegrable multiple of distance to the power −β, since β>r.

The contracted intersections with closed j-balls are compact convex neighborhoods inside U. They increase since the intersections and scaling factors increase and the intersections contain the origin. For any fixed x in U, x/(1−1/j) eventually lies in U and has norm at most j, proving exhaustion. On each compact neighborhood the cutoff density is bounded and upper semicontinuous, and its extended inverse power for p=r is the convex increasing power β/(r+1) of the original inverse power.

The compact radial lemma with p=r gives the cutoff radii after multiplication by r^(1/r). Polar integration gives the volume bound M. The convex hull of the shared equatorial disk with a candidate point bounds its norm uniformly by the cone volume. Convexity and the shared ball show that contracting any point of the closed union by 0<θ<1 puts it inside some cutoff body, so taking radial suprema recovers the closed-union radius on every ray. Monotone convergence gives the full integral on each ray; polar integration then transfers every Borel angular mass, including through-anchor closed halfspaces.

For each boundary point x, the ray parametrized by tx has weighted integral 1/r by homogeneity. With the factor r absorbed into the density, both ray quantiles have positive derivatives 1/[R_i^(r−1) f̃(R_i x_i)]. Differentiating their weighted harmonic mean gives exactly T Σ a_i X_i^β/R_i^r. Both a_i are positive, sum to one, and give T=a_1R_1+a_2R_2. The corresponding point Tz is a convex combination of points in U.

Weighted Hölder gives (Σ a_i X_i)^β ≤ (Σ a_i X_i^β/R_i^r)(Σ a_i R_i^s)^(β−1). With s=r/(β−1) strictly between zero and one, strict Jensen applies when the radii differ. Such a difference persists on an interval by continuity. The increasing C¹ change of variable T on compact probability subintervals maps into the positive z-ray, so its mass integral over all levels is bounded above by one, including unbounded support. A strict interval would force it above one. Identical quantiles give equal endpoints and pointwise equality of the continuous ray densities before the endpoint.

For r≥2 the sphere is connected, so finite closed facets cannot split into two disjoint nonempty unions. Common points of meeting facets propagate the profile and endpoint to every boundary point. Scaling along boundary rays identifies U and the almost-everywhere density. Convexity on a ray gives convexity of the profile inverse power. Every sx for s<t is in tB, a convex hull of vertices with common inverse-power value at t, so the profile inverse power is nondecreasing. The radial normalization is r∫t^(r−1)F(t)dt=1.

dependencies.mapping: Apply with p=r to the bounded upper-semicontinuous compactly supported f_j, positive on a neighborhood of the origin. Its extended f_j^(−1/(r+1)) is convex by the increasing convex power of the original positive inverse power restricted to the convex cutoff set. The lemma makes the threshold-one gauge body convex with the origin interior, and dilation by r^(1/r) gives the displayed radius.

overlap.comparison: This fact constructs the gauge body under compact-support and upper-semicontinuity hypotheses at the radial exponent. The draft uses it to handle general integrable strict inverse-power densities at an interior anchor, proves angular transfer, and adds equality rigidity when the resulting body is a polytope. The compact gauge theorem does not identify those ray laws.
